source.version: Conference proceedings paper, ICCMETS 2026; copyright 2026, printed pages 179-190. The saved PDF gives no dated version history or DOI.
source.title_on_document: Generative AI and Student Creativity: Cognitive Scaffolding Tool or Constraint on Originality? An Empirical Investigation in Vietnamese Higher Education

supplement.where: No supplement or online appendix for this paper is referenced in the complete PDF. The 'Appendix of Algorithmic Contribution' in Table 4 is a proposed student deliverable (PDF p. 11, printed p. 189).
supplement.holds: Not stated. The saved PDF contains the main text, Tables 1-4, and references; no supplementary statistics are identified.

paper_design_summary: The paper reports a randomized laboratory experiment comparing unaided control, unconstrained LLM access, and structured use of the same interface, with 480 Vietnamese undergraduates analyzed (PDF pp. 4, 6, Section 3.1 and Table 1). In a 90-minute session they proposed solutions to microplastic contamination and wrote a 600-word campaign brief; raters scored the outputs and embeddings measured similarity across students. The structured protocol required initial unaided ideas, AI critique, and synthesis without copying; no subsequent task after AI removal is reported.

studies.label: Three-arm laboratory experiment: alternative solutions and campaign briefs

arms.name: Unaided Control
arms.description: Creative tasks with no digital devices, search engines, or AI interfaces.

arms.name: Unconstrained GenAI Access
arms.description: Unmonitored access to an LLM interface (GPT-4o / Claude 3.5 Sonnet), told 'You may use the AI tool in any manner you choose to complete this task.'

arms.name: Structured Scaffolding
arms.description: Same LLM, used under the Cognitive Anchor-Rebound Protocol: Phase A at least three own ideas before opening the interface; Phase B critique and counter-factual prompts; Phase C synthesis without copying AI text.

participants.exclusions: Not reported. Section 3.1 lists 160 students per randomized experimental condition; Table 1 reports 160 analyzed students per arm and N = 480 analyzed students. No separate participant-flow account or allocation procedure is supplied; matching counts are not an explicit report of zero exclusions.
participants.who: Undergraduates from Vietnam National University (Hanoi), The University of Danang, and Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HUTECH); 160 each in humanities and social sciences, business and management, and design, media and technology; 58.3% female; mean age 20.4 (SD 1.35).
participants.quote: A total of 480 undergraduate students participated across three broad disciplinary clusters.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 182), Sections 3.1-3.2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 183), sampling matrix; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 184), Table 1 for analyzed counts.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o / Claude 3.5 Sonnet (LLM interface; which model each participant used is not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: Unconstrained arm: free use of GPT-4o / Claude 3.5 Sonnet through an LLM interface. Structured arm: the same interface under the Cognitive Anchor-Rebound Protocol, with at least three own ideas before opening it, critique and counter-factual prompts, and synthesis without copying AI text. The paper does not say which model each participant used (PDF p. 4, printed p. 182, Section 3.1).

task.description: Task 1: Alternative Solutions Task, proposing sustainable solutions to urban microplastic contamination in the Mekong Delta agricultural belt. Task 2: a 600-word conceptual campaign brief for a socio-technological enterprise addressing rural education equity in Vietnam. See PDF p. 5 (printed p. 183), Section 3.3.
task.duration: Two tasks within one 90-minute timed session (PDF p. 5, printed p. 183, Section 3.3).

outcomes.name: Across-student semantic diversity: mean pairwise cosine similarity and dispersion
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Student submissions were embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large in a paper-stated 1536-dimensional vector space. Similarity was calculated between submissions within the same condition and task; Table 2 also gives dispersion as 1 - CosSim. Higher similarity means less across-person diversity, so contrast directions are coded for diversity. The task, aggregation into analysis observations, SD basis, and inferential unit are not specified; unit and n_units are null. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 183), Section 3.4 item 3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 185), Section 4.2 and Table 2.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity (SD); Semantic Dispersion Index = 1 - CosSim.
diversity_detail.computed_over: All student submissions within the same task and condition, compared pairwise (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4 item 3). Table 2 does not identify the task or explain whether tasks are combined.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The paper prints t(318) = 34.21, p < .001 for Unconstrained GenAI vs Unaided Control. It does not identify the t-test subtype, the observations supplied to it, or what the Table 2 SDs are taken over. Pairwise metric construction does not establish a pair-level inferential analysis; the degrees of freedom do not establish an output-level analysis. No pairwise test is reported for either scaffolded contrast.
diversity_detail.notes: Semantic Distance is explicitly named as primary in Section 4.1 but is absent from Table 1. Table 2 supplies numeric arm means and SDs, and Table 1 supplies people analyzed per arm; this supports the arm_means_sds_ns availability tag, with no claim that the number of similarity observations is known.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Section 3.1 explicitly reports randomized between-subjects assignment to unaided control, unconstrained LLM access, and structured LLM use (PDF p. 4, printed p. 182). Table 1 reports 480 analyzed students, 160 per arm (PDF p. 6, printed p. 184). Six domain experts rated student project briefs for originality, appropriateness, and overall creativity, and embeddings compared student submissions (PDF p. 5, printed p. 183, Section 3.4). The elaboration raters' qualifications are unspecified, so S1-O6.measure is null, but their scoring of submissions is explicit and criterion 3 remains met. The unresolved statistical discrepancies and method details affect extraction or precision, not these eligibility determinations.

one_line_finding: Unconstrained AI raised fluency (11.45 vs 5.12) but lowered originality (3.41 vs 4.82) and diversity (cosine similarity 0.689 vs 0.412), while scaffolding raised originality (5.44; reported d = 0.61 vs control) and overall creativity (5.51 vs 4.48; PDF pp. 6-7, Tables 1-2).
open_questions: Fluency conflicts: Abstract reports F(2,477) = 48.21, eta^2 = .168 (PDF p. 1), whereas Table 1 reports F(2, 477) = 284.15, eta^2 = .543 (PDF p. 6); both give p < .001. The correct analysis is not established by the PDF.
Originality effect conflicts: unconstrained vs control d = -0.58 in Abstract (PDF p. 1), but d = -1.34 in Section 4.1 and Discussion (PDF pp. 6, 9). Both are preserved without recomputation.
The diversity analysis unit, aggregation into observations, SD basis, and t-test subtype are not given (PDF pp. 5, 7). The pairwise definition and reported t(318) do not resolve these omissions.
The task underlying each TTCT score and Table 2 similarity statistic is not identified. CAT ratings are explicitly of project briefs (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4).
The exact random allocation procedure and any attrition or exclusions are not described; stratified random sampling concerns recruitment (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2).
Which participants used GPT-4o versus Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and whether model choice was assigned, is not stated (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).

Section 4.1 names four primary dependent variables, but Table 1 lists six variables and no Semantic Distance row; the omnibus result is Pillai's Trace = 0.941, F(12,946) = 68.34, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .470 (PDF p. 6). The actual MANOVA specification needs clarification.

Table 3 Model 3 prints Unconstrained Prompt Count -.241 without a star and Iterative Counter-Prompts .389* (PDF p. 7), whereas Section 4.3 gives p < .01 and p < .001 respectively (PDF p. 8). The printed star legend is also malformed: '* p < .05,  p < .01, * p < .001'. Correct significance levels cannot be selected from the PDF.

Regression prose says predictors accounted for 45.8% of explained variance while printing R^2 = .468; Table 3 gives R^2 = .468 and adjusted R^2 = .458 (PDF pp. 7-8). The intended variance claim is unclear.

The unlabeled-status ASCII distribution graphic places control and scaffolded originality higher than their Table 1 means (PDF p. 7 vs p. 6). Whether it is only schematic is not stated; the record uses the printed table values.
The final reference entry ends at 'Bose#' and the PDF stops at printed p. 190 (PDF p. 12). The saved document supplies no continuation or supplement reference.
The 71% recurring-theme result has no essay denominator, explicit coding rule, comparator, or uncertainty (PDF p. 8, Section 5.2).

The occupations and domain expertise of the two blinded, trained TTCT raters are not stated (PDF p. 5, printed p. 183, Section 3.4 item 1; full PDF checked). S1-O6.measure is null because the source does not establish lay/crowd versus expert status; output scoring remains confirmed.
notes: The complete markdown (479 lines) and all 12 PDF pages were read; there are no appended research appendices. All recorded paper numbers were checked against PDF text, with Tables 1-3 recovered using PyMuPDF find_tables. Printed pages 179-190 correspond to PDF pages 1-12. Four scaffolded-versus-unconstrained comparisons present only in B (appropriateness, fluency, flexibility, elaboration) are retained. Omnibus ANOVA statistics are labeled as three-arm tests; they do not supply pairwise significance. Descriptive directions are distinguished from pairwise tests. The qualitative 71% recurring-theme outcome is included without a comparative estimate. The 88.4% adoption-of-an-AI-option finding (PDF p. 8, Section 5.1) concerns AI-use/fixation behavior and is not coded as a separate creativity score. Table 3 concerns process predictors of the already-listed originality outcome among 320 AI users (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3), not an additional randomized contrast or independent sample. The qualitative interviews involved 36 participants, 12 per condition (PDF p. 5, Section 3.5), from this same experiment. Preregistration, data/code URLs, and sample overlap are not reported. Primary-status coding follows the paper's explicit primary-variable list, not an inferred preregistration. The reconciliation counts refer to substantive differences between A and B. Shared source contradictions remain in open_questions and the relevant reported fields; resolving a difference about which caveat to retain does not resolve the underlying statistical inconsistency. Null for the diversity inferential unit implements the instruction not to guess; its permitted categorical alternatives cannot be distinguished from the source. Finalization: the elaboration measure category is null because the document does not establish lay/crowd or expert rater status under the codebook; the reported rater description is retained. All pre-existing open questions and the unresolved diversity-unit reconciliation difference are assessed in final.open_items. Challenge-resolution counts refer only to checker problems; they do not count the separate open reporting items. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged.

open_items.item: Fluency conflicts: Abstract reports F(2,477) = 48.21, eta^2 = .168 (PDF p. 1), whereas Table 1 reports F(2, 477) = 284.15, eta^2 = .543 (PDF p. 6); both give p < .001. The correct analysis is not established by the PDF. Author confirmation of the intended fluency analysis would settle the conflicting statistics; the conflict affects effect extraction, not eligibility.

Originality effect conflicts: unconstrained vs control d = -0.58 in Abstract (PDF p. 1), but d = -1.34 in Section 4.1 and Discussion (PDF pp. 6, 9). Both are preserved without recomputation. Author confirmation of the intended originality contrast and standardized effect would settle the conflict; output scoring and eligibility are already established.

The diversity analysis unit, aggregation into observations, SD basis, and t-test subtype are not given (PDF pp. 5, 7). The pairwise definition and reported t(318) do not resolve these omissions. Also covers the unresolved reconciliation difference for studies[0].outcomes[6].unit and diversity_detail.uncertainty. The authors would need to identify the observations, aggregation, SD basis, and test. This affects diversity-effect precision and pooling, not paper eligibility.

The task underlying each TTCT score and Table 2 similarity statistic is not identified. CAT ratings are explicitly of project briefs (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4). The authors would need to map each reported score to its task and describe any combination across tasks; both tasks produce eligible creative outputs.

The exact random allocation procedure and any attrition or exclusions are not described; stratified random sampling concerns recruitment (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2). The authors would need to provide the allocation procedure and participant flow. The explicit randomized design and 480 analyzed students already establish criteria 1 and 2, so this reporting gap does not make eligibility unclear.

Which participants used GPT-4o versus Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and whether model choice was assigned, is not stated (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1). The authors would need to identify model use by participant and how model choice was determined. Both named interfaces provide generative-AI assistance, so this concerns intervention detail rather than eligibility.

Section 4.1 names four primary dependent variables, but Table 1 lists six variables and no Semantic Distance row; the omnibus result is Pillai's Trace = 0.941, F(12,946) = 68.34, p < .001, partial eta^2 = .470 (PDF p. 6). The actual MANOVA specification needs clarification. The authors would need to specify the MANOVA dependent-variable set and corresponding analysis output. This affects statistical interpretation, not the presence of eligible output scores.

Table 3 Model 3 prints Unconstrained Prompt Count -.241 without a star and Iterative Counter-Prompts .389* (PDF p. 7), whereas Section 4.3 gives p < .01 and p < .001 respectively (PDF p. 8). The printed star legend is also malformed: '* p < .05,  p < .01, * p < .001'. Correct significance levels cannot be selected from the PDF. The authors would need to supply corrected significance labels or regression output. These process-predictor results are not required for eligibility.

Regression prose says predictors accounted for 45.8% of explained variance while printing R^2 = .468; Table 3 gives R^2 = .468 and adjusted R^2 = .458 (PDF pp. 7-8). The intended variance claim is unclear. The authors would need to clarify the intended variance statement and its relation to the reported regression models. This affects regression interpretation, not eligibility.

The unlabeled-status ASCII distribution graphic places control and scaffolded originality higher than their Table 1 means (PDF p. 7 vs p. 6). Whether it is only schematic is not stated; the record uses the printed table values. The authors would need to confirm whether the graphic is schematic or supply a corrected figure. The numeric tables remain the extraction source; the graphic does not decide eligibility.

The final reference entry ends at 'Bose#' and the PDF stops at printed p. 190 (PDF p. 12). The saved document supplies no continuation or supplement reference. The authors would need to supply a complete reference list or corrected proceedings PDF. The truncated bibliography does not remove the methods and results establishing eligibility.

The 71% recurring-theme result has no essay denominator, explicit coding rule, comparator, or uncertainty (PDF p. 8, Section 5.2). The authors would need to supply the essay denominator, coding rule, and any comparison or uncertainty. This limits use of the descriptive recurring-theme finding; other output scores establish criterion 3.

The occupations and domain expertise of the two blinded, trained TTCT raters are not stated (PDF p. 5, printed p. 183, Section 3.4 item 1; full PDF checked). S1-O6.measure is null because the source does not establish lay/crowd versus expert status; output scoring remains confirmed. The authors would need to identify the raters' qualifications to settle the measure category. Human scoring of submissions and the separate expert CAT outcomes already establish criterion 3.
